author: Arjay McCandless
title: System Design Architecture Patterns Cheat Sheet
summary: Most modern system architectures rely on standard design patterns categorized by specific scaling and reliability needs. Common architectural solutions are outlined for scaling reads, scaling writes, real-time data, long-running processes, fault tolerance, and separating read/write pipelines.
transcript: Something I wish I knew when I started learning system design is that most systems follow the same exact patterns. If you wanna scale reads, you can reach for caching, read replicas, or database indexing. If you wanna scale writes, you can reach for batching, sharding, or asynchronous writes. If you need real-time data, think WebSockets, server-sent events, or long polling. For long-running processes, you have message queues, worker pools, and workflow engines. For failures and reliability, you want retries with backoff, idempotency, circuit breakers, and self-healing. And if you need to separate reads and writes, you can apply a CQRS pattern. If you want to learn this stuff and practice every single day, you can do it on my app Devmaxx. Hiring for both interns and full-time roles is picking up right now, so it's the perfect time to get sharp on these skills. Comment dev for the link.

title: 5 Things You Need To Do Before Publishing Your Roblox Game
summary: Before releasing a Roblox game, developers should polish the first five minutes of onboarding and test gameplay across all supported platforms like mobile and console. transcript: 5 things you need to do before you publish a Roblox game. Starting with number one: testing the first 5 minutes of your gameplay. Your onboarding within the first 5 minutes is extremely crucial. You want to make sure your player knows what they're supposed to do within the first 5 minutes, why they should keep playing, what they're working towards, and the progression as well. And then number two is testing your game on all platforms. This is something I'm guilty of. The first game I ever published, bro, mobile players struggled a lot. There were certain buttons they couldn't press because I had like a certain tween and then when you press it, it did the little animation. It's just stupid shit like that that really fucked up the process of my game. So make sure you test on console, make sure you test on mobile, PC, VR, anything, bro. Just do everything you can to make sure it's good on all platforms. Coming in at number three is make sure your visuals look really good before the player clicks on your game. This is extremely important. As a graphic designer, I work in the music industry. I work with a lot of rappers, a lot of artists, etc. In the term and the saying that we have is what you see before you hear. The same thing applies to Roblox: what you see before you play. Make sure your icon, your thumbnail, your description, your title is really appealing. And if you have the money or the budget to get a trailer made for your game, I highly recommend that. Like do that. You need to do a trailer for your game. Like it's really good. And at number four is build a really good progression loop. Make sure the core features of your game are really good. Players always need something that they continuously grind and chase within the game, bro, or else it'll be really fucking boring. There's six things and six steps I really follow when it comes to making a new game every single time: 1. Play, 2. Earn, 3. Upgrade, 4. Unlock, 5. Flex, 6. Repeat. Those six things should always be a core fundamental within your game. What that would essentially look like for a simulator, let's say a simulator, people would need better equipment. For a driving game, people want better and faster looking cars. For a fighting game, people want better equipment, better abilities, and better animations. Like y'all got emotes, it's really dope. There's always something for you guys to chase and some something for the players always have to fight... All right. Coming in at number five is break your game before your players do. And if you had a game where it was really vulnerable to exploits, people could duplicate cash, equipment, fly around, just overall just cheat the game, and it really pisses your players off. Hire a QA lead and get a team of 5 to 10 testers depending on how big your game is and how hard it is to find a bug, to go through and test the onboarding process, make sure everything is smooth, and make sure the gameplay is really good, make sure that there's little to no bugs on different platforms. title: Why You Shouldn't Copy Big Brand SEO and How to Beat Them
summary: Big brands often rely on high domain authority rather than best-practice SEO, which can lead to traffic drops when violating spam guidelines like keyword stuffing. transcript: Google has a section in their spam guidelines called Keyword Stuffing: "It refers to the practice of filling a webpage with keywords in an attempt to manipulate rankings in Google, repeating the same words or phrases so often that it sounds unnatural." author: level5esper
title: How to Relearn DSA from Zero
summary: This video outlines a strategy for mastering Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) that focuses on problem recognition and reasoning rather than relying on curated LeetCode or NeetCode lists. It recommends using the USACO Guide to build core algorithmic tools and AtCoder for granular, untagged practice.
transcript: Maguri here. If I had to relearn DSA from zero, this is how I would do it. I would use two resources that very few people talk about. Let me explain. LeetCode and NeetCode are popular because they're convenient, but I wouldn't use either as my main way to learn. Easy, Medium, and Hard are coarse labels, so it's hard to track your actual level, and a roadmap tells you the topic before you have to recognize it. That ecosystem compounds the problem: repetitive questions with little transferable reasoning, AI-generated editorials written for engagement, and beginners teaching other beginners bad habits. Start with the USACO Guide. Bronze and core Silver teach reusable tools and techniques: prefix sums, binary search, two pointers, sorting, graph traversal, and why each one works. After each topic, close the guide and solve a few sample problems under that topic. Then gradually introduce untagged problems, and record the observation you missed, because that is what transfers. Then use AtCoder for randomized practice. Its granular difficulty estimates keep you near the boundary where the problems are difficult enough to teach you, but still solvable. You might be thinking, 'I only want to pass interviews. Why are you sending me to competitive programming sites?' Because interviews test whether you can solve unseen problems. USACO teaches the core ideas, and AtCoder tests whether you can apply them without being told the topic. A roadmap only lists the topics. Use it as your entire curriculum, and you miss the depth that makes those ideas transferable. Send this to a friend who swears by NeetCode 150, and follow me if you want to get cracked at DSA.
caption:
If I had to relearn DSA from zero, this is how I'd do it. (NOT NeetCode 150).

Every influencer out there only talks about "sheets", "roadmaps", "youtube videos". None of them actually compared all the platforms out there, and it does not teach the depth you need to solve unseen problems.

I've tried over 20+ platforms and I'll tell you exactly the best ones, and why.

I’d use the USACO Guide to build the tools, then AtCoder to calibrate difficulty. Start with tagged examples. Gradually remove the tags. That trains the part interviews actually test: solving a problem you haven’t already classified.

transcript: What is USACO Guide? Do you know what USACO Guide is? It's a free site that teaches you DSA in order, and it explains each topic before you touch the problems. Introduction to Prefix Sums. Computing range sum queries in constant time over a fixed 1D array. It has high-quality written solutions, and again, reading an editorial has plenty of benefits over watching someone else think through a video solution. Our Mission: The USACO supports computing education in the USA and worldwide by identifying, motivating, and training high-school computing students at all levels. It's aimed at high schoolers doing USACO, so it's not meant to be hard. And if you think competitive programming doesn't help in interviews, well, a lot of the guide's problems are literally LeetCode problems with a different name: Counting Rooms is 200. Number of Islands, Minimizing Coins is 322. Coin Change, Static Range Sum Queries is 303. Range Sum Query - Immutable. USACO Guide is community-managed and written by top USACO contestants, including Benjamin Qi, who won the IOI twice and worked at Citadel Securities and now at Anthropic. There's also many strong contestants, like William Lin, who's pretty much LGM, perfect score in IOI, and had a couple famous YouTube videos. The topics are more granular. For example, backtracking is just one section of its Complete Search with Recursion module, right after subsets and permutations. Each module lists its prerequisites, and the ones you can skip say optional in the title, like Hashmaps in Gold. It follows USACO's four divisions. Bronze is the basics, like complete search, sorting, and your first graphs. Then Silver adds prefix sums, binary search, and graph traversal. Gold even gives dynamic programming separate modules, like knapsack, bitmasks, and trees, and Platinum is probably stuff you don't have to worry about. Every module explains the idea with code in C++, Java, and Python, and then gives you practice problems. And lots of them have a written solution that explains why it works. Do the starred problems first, because the guide recommends those. Feel free to skip hard problems, and I wouldn't worry about solving problems in order. For interviews, I'd do Bronze and Silver, then the dynamic programming and graph modules in Gold. If Gold is too hard, do the dynamic programming and graph sections on CSES first, since they're short standard problems like counting coin combinations. Do you know what USACO Guide is?

It's a free, community-run site written by top USACO contestants, including two-time IOI winner Benjamin Qi. It's made for high schoolers, and a lot of its problems are LeetCode problems with a different name: Counting Rooms on CSES is Number of Islands, and Minimizing Coins is Coin Change.

title: Optimizing Page Load Performance with Native HTML Lazy Loading
summary: Browsers by default download all page images simultaneously upon load, causing unnecessary network overhead and degrading Core Web Vitals. Adding the native HTML attribute loading="lazy" to image elements defers offscreen downloads until users scroll near them.
transcript: Have you ever noticed this? When a website has lots of images and you open or reload the page, it can take longer to load. That's because the browser starts downloading every image at once, even the ones you can't see yet. This creates unnecessary network requests, affects page performance, and can hurt your Core Web Vitals. The solution is surprisingly simple: just add one HTML attribute, loading="lazy". And if I add it to my HTML, here's what happens. Now the browser only loads the images that are visible on the screen. As the user scrolls, the remaining images load automatically. One small HTML attribute can make your website much smarter. Follow for more web development tips.
caption:
Most Developers Forget This HTML Attribute!

Did you know you can improve your website's performance with just one HTML attribute? 

Instead of downloading every image at once, use loading="lazy" to load images only when they're about to appear on the screen. This reduces unnecessary network requests and helps improve page performance, especially on image-heavy websites.

💡 A small HTML attribute can make a big difference.
